title: How Product Placement Supports Clinical Hand Hygiene
excerpt: Product placement supports clinical hand hygiene when alcohol-based hand rub is positioned at or near the point of care, supplies are visible and reachable, and placement considers workflow, maintenance and safety.
content_html:
Hand-hygiene product placement affects whether workers can act at the correct moment without interrupting care. Good placement connects the product directly to the workflow that creates the hand-hygiene indication.

Place hand rub near the point of care

WHO recommends point-of-care availability of alcohol-based hand rub. Bedside or other care-zone access reduces the need to walk away from the patient to perform hand hygiene.

Visible and reachable is better than merely present

A dispenser may exist in the room but still be functionally inaccessible if it is hidden, blocked, empty or positioned away from the work sequence.

Map placement to care flow

Consider where staff enter, prepare for care, move between patients, handle shared equipment and leave the care zone. Product placement should support these transitions.

Keep handwashing resources available too

Alcohol-based hand rub does not replace sinks, soap and drying supplies for situations that require handwashing, such as visibly soiled hands.

Placement must support maintenance

Dispensers should be inspectable and easy to service. Empty or malfunctioning units should be identified through routine checks rather than discovered at the moment of care.

Placement must also meet safety requirements

Alcohol-based hand rub is a regulated product with storage and dispenser-placement requirements. Facilities should follow applicable fire, building and manufacturer guidance rather than improvising locations.

Practical takeaway

Good placement makes the correct hand-hygiene action the easy action: visible, reachable, reliable and positioned where care actually occurs.

References

  1. WHO — Hand Hygiene Implementation Tools.
  2. CDC — Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices.
  3. WHO — Alcohol-Based Handrub Risks and Hazards.
